discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: An upper-level ridge will position over the region this evening before waning over the weekend. An active pattern will lead into next week as a series of frontal systems bring widespread precipitation, breezy winds, and the potential for minor coastal flooding.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An upper-level ridge will position over the region this evening before waning over the weekend. Areas of fog will be the main concern until the next disturbance arrives Saturday evening with light lowland rain and mountain snow showers. An active pattern will lead into next week as a series of frontal systems bring widespread precipitation, breezy winds, and the potential for minor coastal flooding.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Saturday night)
paragraphs: An upper-low over OR and N CA will dissipate as an upper-ridge builds into the region tonight. Weak surface gradients, high pressure, and longer nights will promote low clouds and fog development across much of western WA. Visibility could sink to a quarter- mile, especially in areas prone to foggy conditions such as river valleys. Overnight lows are forecast to drop into the upper upper 20s to upper 30s where freezing fog is likely for colder spots such as the southwest interior.

As alluded to, a foggy start to the day on Friday but it'll give way to mostly clear skies in the afternoon. The upper- ridge axis will be just offshore as yet another dry day is in store. High temperatures are on track to be slightly below average for mid-November with highs in the mid to upper 40s. Upper-ridge axis becoming firmly overhead Friday evening as the pattern gently progresses. Friday night almost a carbon copy of Thursday's with another round of foggy weather in concert with min temps in the upper 20s to upper 30s.

An upper-low will position offshore on Saturday, forming a Rex Block as it interacts with a high center in northern BC. This set up will allow for a sub 990 mb surface low to meander offshore the WA coast throughout much of the weekend. PoPs are favored to increase on Saturday evening as light lowland rain showers and mountain snow showers (snow levels around 2,000 ft) return to the forecast. Precipitation amounts are expected to be not impactful.

sections.title: Long term (Sunday through Thursday)
paragraphs: Aforementioned upper-low will continue into Sunday maintaining a chance of showers. It'll finally get ingested into the mean flow on Monday as a broad upper-trough encompasses much of the NE PAC. Models are picking up on the potential for a well-organized frontal system deepening offshore Monday night into Tuesday. This will open up the pattern to a parade of disturbances, maintaining an active pattern into the middle of next week. Here we could see widespread precipitation, breezy winds and the potential for minor coastal flooding as surface low pressure interacts with high astronomical tide along.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: An upper level ridge will build into the region tonight into Friday with northeasterly flow aloft becoming northerly. Light surface winds and mostly clear evening skies will be favorable for low cloud and fog formation overnight. Widespread LIFR ceilings and surface visibility below 3 statute miles are expected overnight into Friday morning across south Puget Sound and the Southwest Interior. Areas of similar conditions will be also be found in outlying river valleys, the Chehalis Gap, and around the central/north Sound. Most areas are expected to scatter out toward 19Z though the stratus may hang on longer in the extreme south Sound. High level moisture will begin to increase by afternoon and evening ahead of an approaching upper trough offshore.

KSEA...Conditions look favorable for low cloud and/or fog formation and probabilistic guidance is fairly high with fog. Quick look at REFS shows greater than 90% probability of fog by 13Z. 06Z TAF issuance will likely include an LIFR ceiling for a few hours in the morning and some visibility restriction...probably down 2 to 3SM and can edge downward from there if trends look lower. Ceilings should lift by around 18Z or 19Z with some high cloud increasing later in the day. Surface wind light and variable overnight becoming S/SW 4 to 7 knots by morning and continuing into Friday afternoon.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: High pressure will build over the waters tonight through Friday night for mostly benign conditions. Can't rule out areas of fog, particularly for the inland waters tonight and Friday night. The weather pattern will become active again on Saturday with headlines likely continuing into next week. A low pressure system spinning offshore this weekend will bring elevated seas and winds to the waters. Latest REFS probabilities for small craft gusts over the coastal waters and west/central Strait of Juan de Fuca exceed 90%. Additionally, models hint at 60-80% chance for gale gusts over the outer coastal waters. Seas will build to 10-15 feet.

A stronger system will impact the waters Monday through Tuesday. Increased offshore winds are highly likely to bring additional headlines to the waters. Confidence continues to increase with the each model run for gales and possible storm force winds over the coastal waters. Winds will peak on Tuesday with high confidence (90% and higher) for gales and a 60-0% chance of storm force wind gusts over the coastal waters. Moreover, there is a 65-75% chance for gales through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Seas also continue to trend upwards with combined seas now approaching 20 feet over the outer coastal waters. An active pattern will persist well into the middle of next week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: A brief period of dry, calm weather will prevail today and Friday under transient high pressure before an active pattern returns this weekend. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain and mountain snow starting Saturday and continuing through next week. While exact details remain subject to ensemble spread, there is a low 5-10% probability of a stronger low tracking close enough to bring higher impact winds during the middle of next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A brief period of dry, calm weather will prevail today and Friday under transient high pressure before an active pattern returns this weekend. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain and mountain snow starting Saturday and continuing through next week. While exact details remain subject to ensemble spread, there is a low 5-10% probability of a stronger low tracking close enough to bring higher impact winds during the middle of next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Wednesday...Mostly dry conditions expected today and Friday as shortwave ridging moves over the PacNW. Heading into the weekend, another cold front is expected to impact the region, bringing light rain and light mountain snow. Heading into early next week, active weather is expected to continue with several systems moving over the region with a low chance for a strong, more impactful system during the middle of the week.

Cool and dry conditions expected today and Friday as upper level ridging supports a short period of high pressure over the region. The only chance for precipitation today is across the south WA and north OR Cascades where wrap around moisture from a departing area of low pressure could support light rain/snow showers through the evening. Temperatures are unlikely to break out of the mid to upper 40s across the interior lowlands with slightly warmer temperatures in

the low 50s along the coast. Another night of temperatures cooling into the low to mid 30s will support another chance for fog development. The best chances for fog will be along the I-5 corridor in southwest WA, around the Portland metro and throughout the Willamette Valley. Localized spots in the southern Willamette Valley and northern OR coast range could observe some freezing fog as temperatures drop below freezing. This could result in a thin glaze of ice on elevated surfaces such as cars but it is not expected to develop on roadways at this time. Motorist should remain cautious during the morning commute where fog may impede visibility.

The next chance for rain is expected to come on Saturday as a trough over the Gulf of Alaska digs southeast toward the PacNW. Timing and location of the cold front still show some spread among the ensembles. Frontal timing along the coast looks like it will be late Friday night into Saturday morning, moving inland by mid Saturday morning. Rainfall totals are expected to be on the lighter side with chances for 48 hour totals to exceed 0.50 inches Saturday through Monday varying across the forecast area. Chances along the coast have increased to 70% or greater, 30-40% over the coast range and 10- 30% across the interior lowlands. There is also a chance for snow in the Cascades as snow levels drop to 2000-3500 feet Saturday evening. Accumulations over 48 hours are expected to be light with a 40-60% for 2 inches at pass level, higher chances above 5000 feet. Travel conditions could become hazardous at times.

Active weather is expected to continue into next week, exactly how impactful is still unclear given model spread. Another digging trough is expected to move toward the PacNW during the Tuesday through Thursday timeframe. A majority of models have a very strong low developing offshore which would lead to lesser impacts across Oregon and Washington. A small fraction, about 5-10% of members have the low developing closer to the coast which could bring stronger, damaging winds to the forecast area. Another scenario is the main low developing well offshore but a secondary meso-low developing along the cold front which could impact the coast. With a decent amount of spread in the main low development and possibly a secondary low, the overall certainty of a major storm is low but not zero. Details should become clearer in the next few days as models continue to adjust. -19

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00Z Saturday...Satellite imagery and terminal observations as of 2330Z Thursday depicted a lingering low stratus deck over the southern Willamette Valley and portions of the central Willamette Valley, bringing continued IFR ceilings to KUAO and KEUG. Cloud cover has scattered out at the remaining TAF sites.

Later this evening into tonight, calm winds and high pressure will support the redevelopment of widespread low stratus and areas of dense fog across the Willamette Valley. This will bring LIFR to IFR ceilings and/or visibilities to all inland TAF sites tonight through tomorrow morning. Given the low sun angle this time of year, fog and low stratus will struggle to clear out tomorrow afternoon. While most TAF sites should see improvement to VFR by 20-23Z Friday, some TAF sites may not clear out at all tomorrow, especially KEUG.
At the coast, light offshore winds should maintain VFR conditions at KAST and KONP through at least 12Z Friday, before chances for MVFR ceilings increase thereafter.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Mostly clears skies and VFR flight conditions will eventually give way to LIFR flight conditions due to dense fog and low stratus tonight through at least tomorrow morning. The main uncertainty is the exact timing fog will develop tonight and exactly when it will lift tomorrow. The most likely time period for fog and low stratus to develop is between 06-10Z Friday. The most likely time period for fog and low stratus to lift is between 20-23Z Friday. -23

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Weak low pressure centered over the outer waters is resulting in light east-southeasterly winds around 15 kt or weaker. Seas have been holding steady around 10-12 ft at 12-13 seconds, so the Small Craft Advisory has been extended to 4 PM this afternoon for all waters including the Columbia River Bar. Later this evening, northerly winds briefly return as high pressure builds. Seas will also gradually subside to 6-7 ft by Friday morning and persist through late Friday night.

The next system arrives late Friday night into Saturday, returning breezy southerly winds and small craft wind gusts up to 30 kt. There is also a 70-90% chance for isolated gale force wind gusts up to 35 kt across the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore, and a 15-30% chance for the inner waters and Columbia River Bar. Seas gradually build over the weekend as another westerly swell moves in, with high confidence (>90% chance) for seas building to 10 ft or greater, and a 20-40% chance for seas of 15 ft or greater. Active weather continues next week.
Long period swells will also result in a moderate threat for sneaker waves through this weekend. Those visiting the coast should use extra precaution when in or near the water. -10
